shipped_row.boundary_rationale: This unit opens the lyric corpus with the woman's voice addressing the man throughout: the defective 'your loves' object (sweep: 4 verses) surfaces first in טוֹבִ֥ים דֹּדֶ֖יךָ (oshb:Song.1.2, tier: byte, 'your loves [are] better'), a second-masculine-singular possessive suffix, and the unit's third verse opens מָשְׁכֵ֖נִי אַחֲרֶ֣יךָ (oshb:Song.1.4, tier: byte, 'draw me after you'), where the 2ms marker sits on אַחֲרֶ֣יךָ (oshb:Song.1.4, tier: byte) rather than on the imperative's own 1cs suffix. The span's middle verse carries its densest 2ms evidence: שְׁמָנֶ֣יךָ, שְׁמֶ֑ךָ, and אֲהֵבֽוּךָ (all oshb:Song.1.3, tier: byte). The addressee stays constant (2ms 'you') across the span, though בָּ֔ךְ (oshb:Song.1.4, tier: byte) is 2fs in form and 2ms only on a pausal reading, left unsettled with no morphology layer staged; the grammatical person of the speaker separately shifts to the cohortative 'we' of “We will be glad and rejoice in you.” (web:Song.1.4), disclosed as texture below rather than argued as a voice-shift, since no addressee or gender-marked form changes there.

shipped_row.device_notes: The book's opening enallage sits here: Song.1.2 moves from a third-masculine verb ('let him kiss me', web:Song.1.2) into second-masculine-singular address within the same breath, and Song.1.4's 'we will be glad' shifts person again without a gender-marked addressee change; held at medium_low because the literary function of this shifting reference (enallage vs. an unmarked chorus intrusion) is argued rather than settled by any single tier-1 form. The WLC marks a setumah at Song.1.4, disclosed here as single-witness tier-3 corroboration that never drives a cut.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: This row is the book's title line and stands alone as its own parent: “The Song of songs, which is Solomon’s.” (web:Song.1.1) renders שִׁ֥יר הַשִּׁירִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר לִשְׁלֹמֹֽה (oshb:Song.1.1, tier: byte). The verse opens with the construct superlative שִׁ֥יר הַשִּׁירִ֖ים and carries the relative-pronoun clause אֲשֶׁ֥ר לִשְׁלֹמֹֽה (oshb:Song.1.1, tier: byte, 'which is Solomon's', a form occurring exactly once book-wide: sweep 1 verse); no verse before it and no verse after it shares this header form, so the seam at Song.1.1|Song.1.2 rests on the frame architecture rather than on any voice marker.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Song.1.1 as a non-counted title pseudo-verse fused into the opening lyric address was rejected: both witnesses count it as an ordinary verse, and it is the verse the two-parent frame (F1/M) sets apart as the header, distinct from the surrounding lyric corpus.

prev_row.device_notes: Texture: elsewhere the book's relative particle is the she-prefix; the superscription attributes the collection to Solomon. No parashah mark touches this verse in the WLC inventory.

next_row.boundary_rationale: בְּנ֖וֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם (oshb:Song.1.5, tier: byte, 'daughters of Jerusalem') opens a new addressee absent from the preceding unit, marking the start of this run; the woman's self-description as “dark, but lovely” (web:Song.1.5) and her vineyard-keeper account in Song.1.6 (web:Song.1.6) both continue in her voice, addressing the same plural daughters through אַל תִּרְא֨וּנִי֙ (oshb:Song.1.6, tier: byte, 'do not stare at me'). The seam at Song.1.6|Song.1.7 is an addressee flip: that plural address gives way to the 2ms suffix on חֲבֵרֶֽיךָ (oshb:Song.1.7, tier: byte, 'your companions'), addressed to the man. MT 1:7 opens with הַגִּ֣ידָה לִּ֗י (oshb:Song.1.7, tier: byte, 'tell me'); the she-ahavah-nafshi formula that follows it in the same verse is her own formula at all five of its attested sites and so marks voice continuity here, not the shift -- it confirms her voice carries across the seam rather than driving the cut.

next_row.device_notes: A setumah sits at Song.1.4 in the Leningrad text (tier-3, single-witness); it tracks the seam immediately before this unit without arguing it. The Kedar-tent and Solomon-curtain similes are texture, not a boundary driver.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: This span is held as one antiphonal bracket rather than atomized per line: הִנָּ֤ךְ יָפָה֙ רַעְיָתִ֔י (oshb:Song.1.15, tier: byte, 'behold you are beautiful, my love') opens in the man's voice, using his word for her in the final token; הִנְּךָ֨ יָפֶ֤ה דוֹדִי֙ (oshb:Song.1.16, tier: byte, 'behold you are beautiful, my beloved') answers with the mirrored formula and her word for him, confirming the reply is hers, and her turn continues through קֹר֤וֹת בָּתֵּ֨ינוּ֙ אֲרָזִ֔ים (oshb:Song.1.17, tier: byte, 'the beams of our house are cedars') with the 1cp form עַרְשֵׂ֖נוּ (oshb:Song.1.16, tier: byte, 'our couch') and בָּתֵּ֨ינוּ֙ (oshb:Song.1.17, tier: byte, 'our house') continuing her plural possessive with no gender-marked interruption; the verse's other 1cp noun stands as a ketiv/qere pair, ketiv רחיטנו against the qere רַהִיטֵ֖נוּ (oshb:Song.1.17, tier: byte, 'our rafters'), disclosed here rather than claimed at either reading. Song.2.1's self-description אֲנִי֙ חֲבַצֶּ֣לֶת (oshb:Song.2.1, tier: byte, 'I am a rose') carries no gender-marked form and is held rather than attributed. The same mirrored alternation recurs at the far end of the span: כֵּ֥ן רַעְיָתִ֖י (oshb:Song.2.2, tier: byte, 'so [is] my love') is his line, and כֵּ֥ן דּוֹדִ֖י (oshb:Song.2.3, tier: byte, 'so [is] my beloved') is hers, closing the antiphon's second mirrored pair. The bytes run on past this close in the same first-person voice -- חִמַּ֣דְתִּי וְיָשַׁ֔בְתִּי וּפִרְי֖וֹ מָת֥וֹק לְחִכִּֽי (oshb:Song.2.3, tier: byte) continuing into הֱבִיאַ֨נִי֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַיָּ֔יִן וְדִגְל֥וֹ עָלַ֖י אַהֲבָֽה (oshb:Song.2.4, tier: byte) -- with no vocative, no address-vocabulary token, and no gender-marked addressee change at the cut, so the boundary at Song.2.3|Song.2.4 is not itself a voice-shift; it is held because the antiphon's own formal marker, the mirrored address pairs, completes at Song.2.2-Song.2.3, while Song.2.4 onward carries none. The closing seam is carried by bracket completion, a tier-1 driver class standing alongside voice-shift markers: the unit opens on the mirrored address pair הִנָּ֤ךְ יָפָה֙ רַעְיָתִ֔י (oshb:Song.1.15, tier: byte) answered by הִנְּךָ֨ יָפֶ֤ה דוֹדִי֙ (oshb:Song.1.16, tier: byte) and closes on the second mirrored address pair כֵּ֥ן רַעְיָתִ֖י (oshb:Song.2.2, tier: byte) answered by כֵּ֥ן דּוֹדִ֖י (oshb:Song.2.3, tier: byte). The two pairs are a structural mirror, not a byte-identical inclusio -- the opening and closing frames share no run -- and the gendered contrast that distinguishes the pair, הִנָּ֤ךְ against הִנְּךָ֨, is a byte-tier fact only: the two forms share a skeleton (word-bound sweep: 3 verses book-wide), so the contrast does not survive at skeleton tier. Confidence is held at medium_low.
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the exchange through Song.2.4-Song.2.6 to the Song.2.7 adjuration close was considered and engaged from the bytes: the same first-person speaker configuration continues at byte tier past this span's own closing seam (חִמַּ֣דְתִּי וְיָשַׁ֔בְתִּי וּפִרְי֖וֹ מָת֥וֹק לְחִכִּֽי at oshb:Song.2.3 running into הֱבִיאַ֨נִי֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַיָּ֔יִן וְדִגְל֥וֹ עָלַ֖י אַהֲבָֽה at oshb:Song.2.4, tier: byte, both sides), yet it is rejected as the unit's own close because Song.2.4-Song.2.6 carries no antiphonal address-marker at all -- no vocative, no rayati/dodi term, no gendered second-person form -- while this span's own bracket is built entirely from the mirrored hinnakh/hinnekha and rayati/dodi address pairs that close formally at Song.2.2-Song.2.3. A re-cut variant, severing the run so it is not split across the boundary, was also considered and is unavailable at row granularity: spans are verse-granular, so Song.2.3 must fall wholly to one side, and that side carries the antiphon's closing anchor.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: This unit's seam rests on the marked 2fs addressee dropping rather than on any replacing gender-marked first-person form: נַעֲשֶׂה לָּ֔ךְ (oshb:Song.1.11, tier: byte, 'we will make for you'), the 2fs suffix closing the preceding unit, gives way to נִרְדִּ֖י (oshb:Song.1.12, tier: byte, 'my nard'), a gender-unmarked 1cs possessive beside the third-person עַד שֶׁ֤הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ בִּמְסִבּ֔וֹ (oshb:Song.1.12, tier: byte, the melek lexeme); the shift is carried by the disappearance of the marked addressee plus tier-2 voice continuity, not by a gender-marked replacement form, and confidence is held accordingly. The dodi-exact formula anchors the rest of the run twice, דּוֹדִי֙ לִ֔י (oshb:Song.1.13, tier: byte) and דּוֹדִי֙ לִ֔י (oshb:Song.1.14, tier: byte) -- both 'my beloved is to me', her word for the man (sweep: 24 verses book-wide for the dodi-exact form). The two pairs are a structural mirror, not a byte-identical inclusio -- the opening and closing frames share no run -- and the gendered contrast that distinguishes the pair, הִנָּ֤ךְ against הִנְּךָ֨, is a byte-tier fact only: the two forms share a skeleton (word-bound sweep: 3 verses book-wide), so the contrast does not survive at skeleton tier. From Song.2.4 the unit is her continuing first-person voice on a new topic (the banquet hall), opened by וְדִגְל֥וֹ עָלַ֖י אַהֲבָֽה (oshb:Song.2.4, tier: byte, 'and his banner over me is love') and carrying an addressed plural imperative at its own middle verse -- סַמְּכ֨וּנִי֙ בָּֽאֲשִׁישׁ֔וֹת רַפְּד֖וּנִי (oshb:Song.2.5, tier: byte, 'sustain me with raisins, refresh me'), two plural imperatives with first-person-singular object suffixes -- so the unit is not addressee-free; the same plural-imperative-addressee feature is what drives the cut at Song.2.15. The unit closes on the embrace colon quoted from the bytes rather than in translation: וִימִינ֖וֹ תְּחַבְּקֵֽנִי (oshb:Song.2.6, tier: byte, 'and his right hand embraces me'), attested in that witness as “His right hand embraces me.” (web:Song.2.6), immediately before the adjuration formula breaks in at Song.2.7.

The embrace colon's sub-runs שְׂמֹאלוֹ֙ תַּ֣חַת and וִימִינ֖וֹ תְּחַבְּקֵֽנִי (oshb:Song.2.6, tier: byte) recur at MT 8:3 (sweep: 2 verses); the colon is not identical across the two verses even at skeleton tier, since the lamed of לְרֹאשִׁ֔י (oshb:Song.2.6, tier: byte) is present here and absent from רֹאשִׁ֔י (oshb:Song.8.3, tier: byte) -- the recurrence stands at MT 8:3, immediately before the MT 8:4 adjuration, a parallel supporting this unit's own 2:6|2:7 close rather than a rival to it.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: אֶֽחֱזוּ לָ֨נוּ֙ שֽׁוּעָלִ֔ים (oshb:Song.2.15, tier: byte, 'catch us the foxes') is a self-contained plural-imperative couplet, “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that plunder the vineyards; for our vineyards are in blossom.” (web:Song.2.15), with a plural imperative verb and a plural 'our vineyards' possessive that carry no gender marking distinguishing a speaker, and no vocative connects it to either the man's or the woman's address vocabulary used immediately before and after it. A blossom-token chain straddles this unit's own opening seam at skeleton tier: סְמָדַֽר (oshb:Song.2.15, tier: byte) shares the token with סְמָדַ֖ר (oshb:Song.2.13, tier: byte; no ketiv/qere claim made for that verse's own K/Q note), sweeping to 3 verses book-wide (MT 2:13, MT 2:15, and MT 7:13 = WEB 7:12); the isolation survives it because the shared token is a skeleton-tier imagery link, not a voice or formula anchor.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: עָנָ֥ה דוֹדִ֖י וְאָ֣מַר לִ֑י (oshb:Song.2.10, tier: byte, gloss: 'my beloved answered and said to me'), attested in that witness as “My beloved spoke, and said to me,” (web:Song.2.10), frames the quoted second-feminine-singular speech that follows: ק֥וּמִי לָ֛ךְ רַעְיָתִ֥י יָפָתִ֖י (oshb:Song.2.10, tier: byte, 'rise up, my love, my beautiful one') opens it, using his word for her. The quotation continues unbroken through יוֹנָתִ֞י (oshb:Song.2.14, tier: byte, 'my dove'), another vocative addressed to her, closing on “for your voice is sweet and your face is lovely.” (web:Song.2.14) with no addressee change across the span. A blossom-token link straddles this unit's own closing seam at skeleton tier: סְמָדַ֖ר (oshb:Song.2.13, tier: byte; no ketiv/qere claim made for that verse's own K/Q note) and סְמָדַֽר (oshb:Song.2.15, tier: byte) share the token with the sweep returning 3 verses book-wide (MT 2:13, MT 2:15, and MT 7:13 = WEB 7:12), two of the three sites sitting on opposite sides of this closing cut.

next_row.boundary_rationale: דּוֹדִ֥י לִי֙ וַאֲנִ֣י ל֔וֹ (oshb:Song.2.16, tier: byte, 'my beloved is mine, and I am his') is the first of three attested mutual-belonging shapes in the book (sweep: 3 verses), in the his-mine order; Song.2.17 continues in the same first-person voice, held as tier-2 single-speaker corroboration alongside the mutual-belonging formula site rather than on any addressee-free ground. Within Song.2.17 itself the address turns second-masculine-singular: סֹב֩ דְּמֵה לְךָ֨ דוֹדִ֜י (oshb:Song.2.17, tier: byte, 'turn, be like, my beloved'), the final-kaf-plus-qamats suffix on לְךָ֨ contrasting with the final-kaf-plus-sheva second-feminine-singular suffix on מַרְאַ֔יִךְ (oshb:Song.2.14, tier: byte, 'your face'); the unit's own texture therefore carries an addressed imperative, not an interruption-free run, and the same feature drives the cut at Song.2.15. The unit closes on “Until the day is cool, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young deer on the mountains of Bether.” (web:Song.2.17).

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: מִ֣י זֹ֗את עֹלָה֙ מִן הַמִּדְבָּ֔ר (oshb:Song.3.6, tier: byte, 'who is this coming up from the wilderness') opens the mi-zot ascending-question formula (sweep: 2 verses, byte tier: Song.3.6 and Song.8.5), beginning an unattributed third-person description of Solomon's escorted carriage that continues without a gender-marked speaker change through the palanquin's construction (web:Song.3.9-Song.3.10) to its close: צְאֶ֧ינָה וּֽרְאֶ֛ינָה בְּנ֥וֹת צִיּ֖וֹן (oshb:Song.3.11, tier: byte, 'go out and see, daughters of Zion'), an imperative call to a vocative distinct from the daughters-of-Jerusalem pair used elsewhere (sweep: 1 verse for the daughters-of-Zion form).

next_row.boundary_rationale: The verse holds together as the man's garden-invitation address, closing the movement that opened at oshb:Song.4.16: he reports arrival at בָּ֣אתִי לְגַנִּי֮ (oshb:Song.5.1, byte tier) 'I have come into my garden', then shifts within the same verse to a 2mp imperative summons, אִכְל֣וּ רֵעִ֔ים (oshb:Song.5.1, byte tier) 'eat, friends', addressed past the woman to a plural company. The man's own voice is grounded not on that 1cs perfect but on his address vocabulary standing two words later in the same verse, אֲחֹתִ֣י כַלָּה֒ (oshb:Song.5.1, byte tier) 'my sister, bride' — the bride-epithet form (sweep: 5 verses, word-bound) and kallah (sweep: 6 verses) — the tier-1 anchor his address to her carries elsewhere in the same span. The WEB curly-quoted “Eat, friends! Drink, yes, drink abundantly, beloved.” (web:Song.5.1) marks the widened address as corroboration only. Whether that plural summons is the man's own voice turning outward or a poet/chorus frame laid over his invitation is argued from the bytes alone (no tier-1 speaker change the WEB [SPEAKER] apparatus supplies is admitted as evidence); the verse is held as one unit either way since no in-verse marker forces a split narrower than the verse.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: His renewed praise of her opens on the vocative יָפָ֨ה אַ֤תְּ רַעְיָתִי֙ (oshb:Song.6.4, byte tier) 'beautiful are you, my love', using rayati (his word for her) with the 2fs pronoun, and runs through body-part imagery carrying genuine 2fs address forms — עֵינַ֨יִךְ֙ and שַׂעְרֵךְ֙ (oshb:Song.6.5, byte tier) at MT 6:5, שִׁנַּ֨יִךְ֙ (oshb:Song.6.6, byte tier) at MT 6:6, רַקָּתֵ֔ךְ מִבַּ֖עַד לְצַמָּתֵֽךְ at MT 6:7 (oshb:Song.6.7, byte tier) — into a numeric comparison against the royal household at MT 6:8, which carries no address form, and her uniqueness declaration אַחַ֥ת הִיא֙ יוֹנָתִ֣י תַמָּתִ֔י (oshb:Song.6.9, byte tier) 'she is one, my dove, my perfect one'. MT 6:9 turns to third-feminine-singular predication carrying 1cs-possessive epithets rather than continuing the 2fs address, and no address form stands at MT 6:8 or MT 6:9 either. The span closes on the marveling exclamation מִי זֹ֥את הַנִּשְׁקָפָ֖ה כְּמוֹ שָׁ֑חַר (oshb:Song.6.10, byte tier) 'who is this who looks out like the dawn', itself carrying no address form, and closing on אֲיֻמָּ֖ה כַּנִּדְגָּלֽוֹת (oshb:Song.6.10, byte tier) — the identical byte-tier phrase that closes the span's own opening verse, אֲיֻמָּ֖ה כַּנִּדְגָּלֽוֹת (oshb:Song.6.4, byte tier) (byte sweep: 2 verses, MT 6:4 and MT 6:10), a refrain bracket closing the unit it opened. WEB: “You are beautiful, my love, as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.” (web:Song.6.4); “Who is she who looks out as the morning, beautiful as the moon, clear as the sun, and awesome as an army with banners?” (web:Song.6.10). A second recurrence runs alongside the bracket at accent_stripped tier only: בָּרָ֥ה (oshb:Song.6.9) and בָּרָה֙ (oshb:Song.6.10) match once cantillation is stripped, corroborating continuity across the seam without driving the close. No 2fs address form and no gendered-form change stands anywhere across MT 6:8-6:10, so nothing there licenses a cut; the byte-tier inclusio is what closes the unit at MT 6:10. MT 6:9 sits under its own setumah, span-internal, and MT 6:10 closes under a further setumah at the span's back edge, both single-witness and disclosed as corroboration only.

The internal MT 6:7|6:8 join inside the span carries no marked seam either, which the row's confidence reflects rather than resolves.

next_row.boundary_rationale: A short first-person garden-descent narration, אֶל גִּנַּ֤ת אֱגוֹז֙ יָרַ֔דְתִּי (oshb:Song.6.11, byte tier) 'to the nut-tree grove I went down', WEB “I went down into the nut tree grove” (web:Song.6.11), running into the book's hardest line, לֹ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי נַפְשִׁ֣י שָׂמַ֔תְנִי מַרְכְּב֖וֹת עַמִּי נָדִֽיב (oshb:Song.6.12, byte tier) 'I did not know; my desire/soul set me [with] the chariots of my people, a prince/willing one' — the merkavot-ammi-nadiv crux. The verse immediately preceding this span, MT 6:10, closes the praise unit that precedes it: its third-feminine-singular predication, הַנִּשְׁקָפָ֖ה (oshb:Song.6.10, byte tier) 'who looks out', gives way at the seam to the first-person perfect יָרַ֔דְתִּי (oshb:Song.6.11, byte tier) 'I went down' that opens this span — a genuine person-form shift — and MT 6:10 closes under its own setumah division (single-witness) immediately before it.
